data.title: Microsoft pushes its own AI models at Ignite; OpenAI is 10.8% of its revenue
data.description:
Microsoft used its Ignite conference on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, to put its own AI models in front of customers. Chief executive Satya Nadella announced a new family of coding models and a security model, pointed to a chip Microsoft designed itself, and put models from OpenAI and Meta on the same platform.

The company's filings show why it wants more than one supplier. OpenAI accounted for $10.0 billion of Microsoft's revenue last quarter, which is 10.8% of the total, and it owed Microsoft $7.2 billion at the end of September, TECHi's calculation from the quarterly report shows. Microsoft shares were down 2.3% in afternoon trading, against a 1.2% fall in the Nasdaq 100 fund.

What did Microsoft announce?

The headline products are models that carry Microsoft's own name. Code 2 is a family of coding models that Nadella said sits at the frontier of cost and performance for everyday enterprise work. Code 2 Flash is the cheaper version for high-volume tasks. Both are available now in GitHub Copilot. Cyber 2 Flash is a security model, which Microsoft is offering in preview.

Nadella described Code 2 and Cyber 2 Flash as doing frontier-level work at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft did not publish prices in the keynote.

It also widened the menu of other companies' models. OpenAI's GPT 6.2 is coming to Foundry, Microsoft's platform for building AI applications, and Nadella said Meta's latest models are coming too. Microsoft's summary of the event says Foundry now offers more than 11,000 models. A smaller model for routing and classification, Microsoft-Decision-1.1, became generally available, and Nadella said more than 4,000 customers have used it.

Two other announcements point the same way. Microsoft will give trusted customers access to the weights of its models, meaning the underlying parameters, under a program it calls MAI Licensed Weights. And it has a new chip. Nadella said Maia 300 will deliver 40% more tokens per watt than leading systems built on graphics processors, which today mostly means Nvidia's.

Its Cobalt 200 virtual machines, built on Microsoft's own Arm-based processor, are now generally available and due in 24 Azure regions by the end of the year.

On the product side, Microsoft said it now has more than 50 million AI agents registered in Agent 365, its control system for agents, and announced a partnership to bring Salesforce into Copilot.

The rest of the keynote was about running and policing all of this. Perception, a security system built from teams of AI agents that attack, detect and repair, is now generally available. Agent 365 gains an analytics tool that Nadella compared to an accounting system for AI spending. And Microsoft launched an AI Transparency Initiative with 40 organisations, tied to standards work at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology.

How much of Microsoft's business is OpenAI?

More than most investors would guess from the headline numbers, and Microsoft now spells it out.

Because Microsoft holds about 24% of OpenAI, accounting rules treat OpenAI as a related party, and Microsoft's quarterly report discloses what the two do with each other. For the three months to September 30, Microsoft recorded $10.0 billion of revenue from its commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments. Total revenue was $92.3 billion, up 18.8% from a year earlier, an increase of $14.6 billion. OpenAI was therefore 10.8% of the total, a pace of $40 billion a year from one customer.

The second number is what OpenAI owes. Accounts receivable from OpenAI were $7.2 billion at September 30, up from $6.0 billion three months earlier, a rise of 20%. That is 11.6% of everything Microsoft was owed by customers, against 7.4% in June. At the quarter's pace it equals 66 days of OpenAI revenue, a little more than the 62 days for Microsoft's customers as a whole. If OpenAI were paying at the average customer's pace, the balance would be about $6.7 billion.

Microsoft has committed $13.0 billion to its OpenAI investment and had funded $12.0 billion of that by the end of September. The investment added $207 million to net income in the quarter. A year earlier it had subtracted $3.1 billion.

Why does that make Ignite matter?

A customer that is one-tenth of revenue is a strength while it grows and a risk if it slows, switches suppliers or struggles to pay. OpenAI has been signing computing deals with other providers for more than a year, and it released a new model of its own on Tuesday.

Seen that way, the keynote reads as a list of hedges. In-house models for coding and security give Microsoft something to sell that does not depend on OpenAI's roadmap or share revenue with it. Hosting Meta's models next to OpenAI's makes Foundry a marketplace instead of a reseller. A chip of its own lowers the cost of running whichever model the customer picks. Even the small Decision model is built on Gemma, an open model from Google, according to Microsoft's event summary.

Microsoft's reporting has moved the same way. Since the start of this fiscal year it has reported two segments, one of which is called Agents and Infra.

The cost of the strategy is in the same filing. Microsoft spent $39.4 billion on property and equipment in the quarter, about double the $19.4 billion of a year earlier, and equal to 43% of revenue. It holds $683 billion of contracted future revenue, of which it expects to recognise about 30% within twelve months.

What does it mean for Microsoft stock?

Microsoft closed on Monday at $517.99. That values the company at about $3.85 trillion and is 26 times the $19.91 a share that analysts expect it to earn in the fiscal year to June 2027, according to estimates compiled by Nasdaq. The shares were up 7.1% for the year at Monday's close and 6.8% below their November 4 close of $555.80, the highest of the past year.

Tuesday's fall is hard to pin on the keynote. AI stocks were weak across the board ahead of Nvidia's results, though Microsoft fell roughly twice as much as the Nasdaq 100 fund.

The case for the strategy is simple. If customers buy Microsoft's cheaper models for routine work, Microsoft keeps more of each dollar and depends less on a partner that is also a competitor. The case against is that OpenAI's models are why many customers came to Azure in the first place. Selling against a company that supplies a tenth of your revenue is a delicate thing to do well.

TECHi noted in September that Microsoft had begun publishing Azure's revenue while keeping its margin private. The OpenAI figures are a second window that its filings have opened.

One quarter is also a thin base. The filing gives the OpenAI revenue figure for the latest quarter only, with no year-earlier number to set beside it.

What to watch

Prices for Code 2 are the first thing to look for, since a fraction of frontier cost can mean many things. The next quarterly report, due in late January, will show whether OpenAI's share of revenue and of receivables is still rising. Nvidia reports after Tuesday's close, and Microsoft is one of its largest customers as well as, with Maia, a would-be rival. TECHi's Microsoft quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Waymo pulls robotaxis off US freeways after California ban; unit is 0.3% of Alphabet sales
data.description:
Waymo has stopped carrying passengers on freeways in every US market after California's Department of Motor Vehicles banned its driverless cars from the state's freeways, NBC News and Wired reported on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The DMV said the cars pose "an imminent hazard to public safety" after two incidents near San Francisco. Waymo is owned by Alphabet.

For Alphabet's shareholders the direct money is small. Waymo sits in a segment called Other Bets, which brought in $372 million last quarter, 0.3% of Alphabet's revenue, and lost $2.05 billion, according to the company's quarterly report. That is $5.50 lost for every dollar of sales, TECHi's calculation shows. The same report shows Waymo arranged a $5 billion loan in October on its own credit, without a guarantee from its parent.

What did California do?

The DMV issued the ban on November 11, according to NBC News, and it became public on Tuesday. The department cited two recent incidents. In one, three Waymo vehicles drove into an active construction closure on Route 101 on the San Francisco Peninsula, Wired reported. In the other, a Waymo car tried to pass California Highway Patrol officers who were holding back traffic on a San Francisco freeway while a crash was cleared.

The department's reasoning, as quoted by NBC News, is that Waymo's driverless freeway operations are a hazard because its vehicles keep entering active construction zones where workers and equipment are present. It said it had placed similar restrictions on the company after similar incidents earlier this year.

There is no end date. A DMV spokesperson told Wired the ban stays until Waymo shows it has taken effective corrective action. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said it is in contact with the DMV and with Waymo and will take further action as appropriate, NBC News reported.

What did Waymo do?

It went further than the order required. California's ban covers California. Waymo paused freeway routes in all of its markets, and described the step as its own decision. The company said the restriction applies only to freeway service and that it is working to reopen those routes quickly and safely.

Rides on ordinary streets continue in the 15 metropolitan areas where Waymo operates, including parts of Los Angeles, San Diego and the San Francisco Bay Area, according to Wired. Waymo will keep testing on highways with a safety operator behind the wheel. The company pointed out that the construction zone incidents caused no injuries or collisions.

This is not the first time. Waymo began carrying passengers on freeways last year. In June it recalled the software in more than 3,800 robotaxis after at least 13 cases of cars driving into highway construction zones, six in Phoenix in April and seven in San Francisco in May, ABC7 News reported at the time, citing the company and federal filings. Waymo restricted its freeway operations then too.

Federal regulators are also looking again at an older problem. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said last week that it is examining whether a software fix Waymo made after its cars passed stopped school buses has worked, Wired reported. TECHi wrote about that problem last year.

Freeways matter to the business because they shorten longer trips, the kind that link suburbs, airports and city centers. A robotaxi that must stay on surface streets takes longer and serves a smaller area.

How big is Waymo inside Alphabet?

Alphabet does not report Waymo's results separately. It reports Other Bets, a group of smaller businesses whose revenue, the filing says, comes mainly from autonomous transportation services and internet services.

In the three months to September 30, Other Bets had revenue of $372 million, up 8% from a year earlier. Alphabet's total revenue was $127.6 billion, up 25%. Other Bets was 0.29% of the total.

The losses are a different size. Other Bets lost $2.05 billion in the quarter, up 44% from $1.43 billion a year earlier. Over nine months it lost $5.95 billion on revenue of $1.17 billion, and that revenue was flat against the same period of 2025. Alphabet put the larger loss down mainly to employee pay.

Set against the whole company, the loss is manageable. Alphabet's operating income in the quarter was $40.6 billion, so Other Bets consumed about 5% of it. Google Cloud's operating profit alone, $11.1 billion, covers the Other Bets loss more than five times.

Why does the $5 billion loan matter?

The detail that makes the ban more than a local story is in Alphabet's notes on debt. In October, Waymo signed a credit agreement for a $5.0 billion senior secured term loan that matures in October 2032. The interest rate is a benchmark rate plus 5.25 percentage points. The loan is secured on some of Waymo's own assets and subsidiaries, and Alphabet says neither it nor its other subsidiaries guarantee it.

That is the borrowing of a company expected to stand on its own. Alphabet itself raised $28.7 billion in the third quarter through unsecured notes.

On the full $5 billion, the margin alone would cost $262.5 million a year. That is 71% of what all of Other Bets earned in revenue last quarter, or about 18% of its revenue at an annual pace. Lenders who priced that loan in October now face a borrower whose home-state regulator has taken its cars off the freeway, at least for now.

Alphabet's report also shows outside money in its subsidiaries growing. Noncontrolling interests, the stakes other investors hold in businesses Alphabet controls, rose to $6.9 billion at the end of September from $3.4 billion at the start of the year. The report gives the totals, and TECHi did not find a breakdown by subsidiary.

What does it mean for Alphabet stock?

Very little in the numbers, and possibly more in the story investors tell about the company.

Alphabet closed on Tuesday at $280.20, down 1.2% on the day and 5.3% over two sessions. It is down 10.5% this year and 30% below its closing high of $402.62 in May. On the share counts in its latest report the company is worth about $3.44 trillion. Alphabet has made no filing with the SEC about the ban. Its most recent current report is dated November 5.

Tuesday's fall took about $43 billion off that value. The whole of Other Bets, at last quarter's pace, brings in about $1.5 billion a year. A one-day move in the stock was worth 29 years of that revenue, and AI stocks fell broadly on Tuesday, so the ban cannot be read into the price.

The case for caring is that Waymo is Alphabet's most visible AI product outside search and cloud, and investors value it on what it might become. Freeway driving is part of that promise, and this is the second time in six months that construction zones have forced Waymo off the freeway. Its main rival for attention, Tesla, has its own gaps to close, as TECHi has reported.

The case against is scale. Street service continues in 15 metropolitan areas, Waymo says nobody was hurt in the construction zone incidents, and a business that is 0.3% of revenue cannot move Alphabet's earnings in either direction this year.

What to watch

The DMV decides when the ban ends, and it has set a test, not a date. Federal regulators may add steps of their own. Alphabet's next results, expected in late January or early February, will show whether Other Bets' revenue is still flat while its losses grow. TECHi's Alphabet quote page carries the live price.

data.title: US chip rule takes effect as Nvidia halts H200 sales to China, $2.4B last quarter
data.description:
The US Commerce Department's new limits on advanced AI chips take effect on Thursday, November 19, 2026, the day the rule is published in the Federal Register. Nvidia has already gone further than the rule asks. The company has stopped selling its H200 chips to China, interim chief executive Colette Kress said on its earnings call on Tuesday, according to TechCrunch. Semafor also reported the halt.

Nvidia's own filing shows what that business was worth. Shipments of that generation of data center chip to China were $2.4 billion last quarter, its results commentary says. That is 2.1% of revenue, and it equals about a fifth of what Nvidia books from customers based in China. The forecast Nvidia gave on Tuesday already assumed none of it, which changes how that forecast reads. Take the disclosed China shipments out of last quarter and the outlook implies revenue per week rising 6.4%, where the headline comparison gives 4.2%, TECHi's calculation shows.

What takes effect on Thursday?

The rule is called Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors. The Commerce Department filed it on Monday, November 16, and it runs to 117 pages. It takes effect on publication.

It does two things. It requires a US license to export, re-export or transfer advanced AI chips to five countries: Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil. Washington's stated concern is that chips sent there can be passed on to China. TECHi reported on Tuesday that customers based in those countries account for 1.3% of Nvidia's revenue at most.

The second part reaches further. The rule also covers data centers in any country that provide large amounts of computing power to companies headquartered in China and in other countries under US export controls. Data centers already serving such customers have 90 days to obtain a license. Counted from Thursday, that deadline is February 17, 2027.

China's commerce ministry has said it will take countermeasures if the rule goes ahead, as TECHi reported on Wednesday.

What did Nvidia stop?

The H200 is a data center chip from Nvidia's Hopper generation, two generations behind the Rubin systems it has just begun shipping. The White House approved its export in January, Semafor reported, and TECHi reported in August that the first deliveries were running far below what the licenses allowed.

Kress told analysts on Tuesday that Nvidia would no longer sell H200 chips to China, according to TechCrunch's account of the call, as relayed by PCMag. Semafor's account says Nvidia halted the sales as it prepared for closer scrutiny from lawmakers. Former chief executive Jensen Huang is expected to testify to Congress next month, Semafor reported. TECHi has not seen a transcript of the call.

Nvidia's written materials do not announce a halt. They contain two sentences on China. One gives the size of the shipments. The other is in the outlook: Nvidia said it is not assuming any data center computing revenue from China.

The decision follows a week in which the company's dealings with China became a governance question. Nvidia's board has set up a committee to oversee export controls, as TECHi reported on Tuesday.

How much revenue is at stake?

Start with the figure Nvidia gives. Shipments of Hopper data center products to China were $2.4 billion in the three months to October 25.

Nvidia's revenue in the quarter was $115.84 billion, so the shipments were 2.1% of the total. They were 2.2% of data center revenue, which was $107.6 billion.

Set against China alone, they matter more. A supplement filed with the results shows $11.05 billion of revenue from customers headquartered in China, including Hong Kong. The Hopper shipments equal 22% of that. Nvidia does not say how the rest is made up.

That China figure had been recovering. It was $2.97 billion in the same quarter a year earlier. Over nine months it is $23.48 billion, against $16.62 billion.

If the $2.4 billion were repeated every quarter, it would be $9.6 billion a year. One comparison gives a sense of scale. In the same quarter, every customer based outside the United States, Taiwan and China bought $1.6 billion from Nvidia between them. The halted China shipments were half as large again as that.

What does it do to the forecast?

Nothing, on Nvidia's account, because the forecast never included it. The company expects revenue of $130.0 billion this quarter, plus or minus 3%.

That makes the comparison with last quarter uneven. Last quarter's revenue had $2.4 billion of these China shipments in it. This quarter's forecast has none.

TECHi's report on the results noted that the current quarter has 14 weeks, one more than usual, and that revenue per week would rise 4.2% at the midpoint of the forecast. Remove the disclosed China shipments from last quarter and the base falls to $8.73 billion a week from $8.91 billion. The forecast is $9.29 billion a week. On that basis the increase is 6.4%.

At the bottom of Nvidia's range the increase would be 3.2%, and at the top 9.6%.

So the business outside these China sales is growing about two points faster than the headline arithmetic suggested. The halt removes revenue Nvidia had last quarter, and it does not lower what the company told investors to expect.

The larger risk is the part of the rule that covers data centers. PCMag, citing TechCrunch, reported an estimate from the investment bank Jefferies that the restrictions on remote access could cost Nvidia as much as $62 billion of data center revenue next year. Kress said on the call that demand for the Rubin chips would cover a shortfall, according to the same account. For scale, the growth target Kress gave on Tuesday implies revenue of about $741 billion next fiscal year, on TECHi's calculation. The Jefferies figure is 8% of that.

How are the five countries responding?

Carefully. Indonesia's government communications agency said in a statement to the broadcaster CNA on Wednesday that it is reviewing the measure and asking industry how it would affect operations and investment, including in data centers. It said it is open to technical talks on how the rule will apply.

Singapore's prime minister, Lawrence Wong, said the country is prepared to help the United States check how advanced chips are used there, CNA reported. Malaysia has told data centers operating in the country that they must comply with the US rules, Reuters reported.

None of the three has said it will resist. Their data center industries run on American chips.

What does it mean for Nvidia stock?

On the numbers, the H200 decision is small. It is 2% of revenue and it was already outside the forecast. Nvidia closed at $150.96 on Wednesday, its lowest close since June 2025, as TECHi reported.

The case for concern is that the rule is aimed at something harder to measure. Nvidia does not say how much of its revenue comes from data centers abroad that rent capacity to Chinese companies. Customers based outside the United States, Taiwan and China accounted for $1.6 billion last quarter, 1.4% of revenue, but a data center's customers and its owner's headquarters are not the same thing.

The case against is that Nvidia is selling everything it can make. Kress told analysts that demand still far exceeds supply, CBS News reported, and the forecast excludes China and still rises.

What to watch

The 90-day period for existing data centers ends on February 17, 2027. Nvidia's quarterly report, due by December 4, should say more about China than the results release did. Huang's expected appearance before Congress next month will keep the company's past sales there in view, and China has yet to say what its countermeasures will be. TECHi's Nvidia quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Nvidia revenue hits $115.8B, above its forecast; $130B outlook is 4% growth per week
data.description:
Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the three months to October 25, 2026, up 103% from a year earlier and $7.8 billion above the midpoint of its own forecast, according to results released after the market closed on Tuesday, November 17. Earnings were $2.70 a share. It is the first report since Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive.

The outlook is strong on its face and slower underneath. Nvidia forecast revenue of $130.0 billion for the current quarter, which runs for 14 weeks, one more than usual. Per week, that is 4.2% more than last quarter, against the 12% the headline figure suggests. At the gross margin Nvidia forecast, weekly gross profit would be flat, TECHi's calculation shows. The shares rose between 2% and 4% in the first minutes of after-hours trading.

How did Nvidia do against its forecast?

It beat it by a wide margin. In August the company told investors to expect $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, a range that topped out at $110.2 billion. The reported figure of $115.84 billion was $5.7 billion above the top of that range and 7.3% above the midpoint.

Revenue rose 20% from the previous quarter. The gross margin was 74.8%, above the 74.0% Nvidia had forecast. Net income was $65.3 billion, up 105%. Operating expenses rose 57% from a year earlier, which Nvidia put down to spending on computing infrastructure and pay. Earnings of $2.70 a share compare with $1.30 a year earlier. Analysts had expected $2.49, according to estimates compiled by Nasdaq, and Nvidia's adjusted figure was $2.68.

Data center revenue was $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year earlier. Commentary from Colette Kress, who is both interim chief executive and chief financial officer, splits that into $60.1 billion from the largest cloud companies and $47.5 billion from other AI cloud providers, industrial customers and enterprises. The second group nearly tripled in a year. Nvidia said its new Vera Rubin systems have begun shipping and called it the fastest product ramp in its history. Kress's summary in the release was four words: "Our momentum is real."

The result also answers a question the market asked a week ago. When Nvidia's shares fell on November 9, TECHi calculated that the drop was equivalent to revenue coming in about $4.7 billion below the forecast midpoint. It came in $7.8 billion above.

What does the $130 billion outlook really mean?

Nvidia's fiscal fourth quarter ends on January 31, 2027, and the company said its outlook includes an additional week. That matters when comparing it with a 13-week quarter.

The forecast is $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, or $126.1 billion to $133.9 billion. Set against the $115.8 billion just reported, the midpoint is a 12.2% increase. Divide each quarter by its number of weeks and the picture changes. Nvidia took in $8.91 billion a week last quarter. The midpoint of the outlook is $9.29 billion a week, an increase of 4.2%. At the low end of the range the weekly increase is 1.1%, and at the high end it is 7.3%. Revenue grew 20% in the quarter just reported and 18% in the one before.

Margins pull the same way. Nvidia expects a gross margin between 71.0% and 72.0%, down from 74.8%. At the midpoints, gross profit would be $92.95 billion, or $6.64 billion a week, against $6.67 billion a week last quarter. That is a decline of 0.4%. Add the forecast operating expenses of about $11.0 billion and implied operating profit per week falls 1.8%.

Nvidia said the small fall in margin last quarter reflected the start of the Rubin ramp. Its commentary does not give a reason for the larger drop it forecasts. It also widened its forecast band to 3% from 2%.

None of this makes the outlook weak. A company adding $14 billion of revenue in a quarter is still growing fast. But the growth rate that investors will quote, 12%, owes about two-thirds of its size to the calendar.

What happened in China?

Revenue from customers headquartered in China, including Hong Kong, was $11.05 billion, or 9.5% of the total, according to a supplement filed with the results. That is up 40% from $7.88 billion the quarter before. Nvidia said shipments to China of data center products based on its older Hopper design were $2.4 billion.

Customers based in every country other than the United States, Taiwan and China accounted for $1.6 billion, or 1.4%. That group contains the five countries named in the chip export rule the Commerce Department filed on Monday, which TECHi covered earlier on Tuesday.

Nvidia repeated that its outlook assumes no data center computing revenue from China.

What do the documents leave out?

The release and the commentary give no update on the investigation by an independent committee of the board. They do not mention the oversight committee the board created on Tuesday morning, and they set no timetable for finding a permanent chief executive.

The investigation and the search each appear once, in the legal notice at the end. Nvidia lists both among the subjects on which its statements could prove wrong. Neither was in the same notice in August.

One procedural point stands out. Nvidia said it plans to file its quarterly report "in the coming weeks" and published a financial supplement in the meantime. In each of the previous seven quarters, its quarterly or annual report reached the Securities and Exchange Commission on the same day as the results, filing records show.

The quarterly report is where a company describes legal proceedings and updates its risk disclosures. SEC rules give a company of Nvidia's size 40 days from the end of the quarter to file it. That puts the deadline at December 4.

Where is the cash going?

Nvidia returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the quarter through buybacks and dividends. Its board added $150 billion to the buyback authorization in September, leaving $227.3 billion available.

Its commitments grew faster than its revenue. Supply commitments rose to $390 billion from $279 billion in one quarter, mainly to secure memory chips for several years. Commitments to rent cloud capacity and data centers rose to $102 billion from $74 billion. Guarantees that Nvidia has given on behalf of partners carry a maximum exposure of $118 billion, most of it tied to a data center campus in Ohio that will be leased to OpenAI. Customers also took longer to pay. Receivables stood at 64 days of sales, up from 60, which Nvidia put down to the timing of Rubin shipments and to longer payment terms for some large customers.

Investment gains were modest. Nvidia booked $1.8 billion of net gains on equity securities, made up of $2.8 billion of gains on listed stocks and a $1.0 billion net loss on private holdings that included $1.8 billion of impairments. TECHi's reading of Nvidia's 13F on Monday had put the gain on the listed stakes at $1.5 billion to $2.1 billion.

What to watch

Nvidia's call with analysts was scheduled for 5 p.m. Eastern. The questions the documents do not answer are the ones to listen for: why margins are forecast to fall, how the new export rule affects orders, and what the board has decided about its leadership. The quarterly report, due by December 4, will show what Nvidia says about the investigation. Nvidia closed at $155.46 on Tuesday and traded between $159 and $161 in the 20 minutes after the results. TECHi's Nvidia quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Nvidia vs AMD after earnings: Nvidia beat its forecast; the 29-point gap is not closing
data.description:
Nvidia passed the earnings test its shares faced this month, and the gap with AMD has not closed. From the close on November 6 to the close on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, the last before Nvidia's results, Nvidia fell 16.7% and AMD rose 12.1%, Nasdaq prices show. That is a spread of 28.8 percentage points, almost four times the 7.4 points TECHi first measured on November 9. In pre-market trading on Wednesday, after the results, both stocks rose and the spread did not move.

The result is a difference in price that the two companies' numbers do not explain. At Tuesday's close Nvidia traded at 9.9 times the earnings analysts expect next fiscal year, and AMD at 31.4 times, TECHi's calculation from Nasdaq's consensus estimates shows. Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion on Tuesday evening, above the top of its own forecast range.

What was the test, and did Nvidia pass it?

On November 9, Nvidia was falling and AMD rising before the market opened. TECHi's analysis that morning asked what the drop would mean if it were about the coming quarter. With the valuation held constant, Nvidia's fall was equivalent to revenue landing about $4.7 billion below the $108 billion midpoint of its forecast. AMD's rise, on the same arithmetic, needed only about $259 million of extra quarterly sales, a figure inside its own guidance range.

The article set out what to check on November 17. Nvidia's revenue should be compared with its range of $105.84 billion to $110.16 billion, and its adjusted gross margin with a range of 73.5% to 74.5%.

Nvidia cleared both. Revenue was $115.84 billion, $5.7 billion above the top of the range. The adjusted gross margin was 74.9%, above the top of that range too. Adjusted earnings were $2.68 a share. The figure TECHi had modeled from the midpoint of Nvidia's guidance was $2.42, so the result was 11% better.

So the fall was never about the quarter. The same article noted that investors could put a lower value on Nvidia's earnings while a board inquiry was open, whatever the results said. That is what happened. Between the two dates Nvidia's chief executive resigned, the board began looking for a successor, and the Commerce Department issued a new rule on chip exports.

How wide is the gap now?

Nvidia closed at $186.64 on November 6 and at $155.46 on Tuesday. On its diluted share count that is about $754 billion of market value gone in seven sessions. The stock fell in six of the seven, and Tuesday's close was its lowest in a year.

AMD closed at $449.04 on November 6 and at $503.41 on Tuesday. It was not a straight line. AMD rose 13.3% on November 9 alone and reached $585.30 on November 12, up 30% in four sessions. It has since given back more than half of that gain. At its widest, on November 12, the spread between the two stocks was 41 points.

AMD had news of its own in the period. It closed two acquisitions and issued about 15 million shares to pay for one of them, as TECHi reported on Tuesday.

The results arrived after Tuesday's close, so Wednesday is the first chance for the market to respond. Early trading did not change the picture. At 6:39 a.m. Eastern, Nvidia was at $159.89, up 2.9%, and AMD at $514.02, up 2.1%, according to Nasdaq's pre-market quotes. On those prices the spread is unchanged at 28.8 points. A beat that large lifted the rival almost as much as the company that reported it.

What does each stock cost now?

The November 9 article compared the two by dividing each share price by four times a quarter's adjusted earnings. On that measure Nvidia was at 18.3 times and AMD at 39.4 times.

Run it again with Tuesday's closing prices. Using the $2.68 Nvidia has now reported, Nvidia is at 14.5 times. Using the same $2.92 modeled for AMD's December quarter, AMD is at 43.1 times. The stock that beat its forecast became cheaper. The one that has not yet reported became more expensive.

Analysts' forecasts give the same answer. Nasdaq's consensus puts Nvidia's earnings at $15.63 a share for the fiscal year that ends in January 2028 and AMD's at $16.04 for calendar 2027. The two figures are almost identical. The share prices are $155.46 and $503.41.

Looking a year further out does not close the difference. The consensus has AMD earning $25.07 a share in 2028 and Nvidia $21.53 in the year to January 2029. On those figures AMD trades at 20 times earnings and Nvidia at 7, though fewer analysts publish estimates that far ahead.

Another way to see it: for AMD to trade on Nvidia's multiple at Tuesday's price, it would need adjusted earnings of about $8.68 a share every quarter. Its guidance for the December quarter implies $2.92. On November 9 the equivalent figure was $6.29.

Why would investors pay three times as much for AMD's earnings?

Growth is the usual answer, and analysts do expect more of it from AMD. The consensus has AMD's earnings rising 131% in 2027, against 68% for Nvidia in its next fiscal year. Estimates for AMD are also moving up. Of 20 analysts covering its 2027 earnings, 19 have raised their forecasts recently, Nasdaq's data shows.

The reported numbers are less one-sided. AMD's revenue in the September quarter was $13.4 billion, up 45%, and it earned $2.09 a share on an adjusted basis. Nvidia's revenue in its latest quarter was $115.8 billion, almost nine times as much, and its net income of $65.3 billion compares with $2.4 billion at AMD. AMD's quarterly report shows data center revenue of $8.5 billion in the September quarter, up 97% from a year earlier. Nvidia's data center revenue was $107.6 billion in its latest quarter, up 110%. Nvidia is growing faster from a base more than 12 times as large. The $18.6 billion it added to data center revenue in a single quarter is more than twice what AMD's data center segment brought in.

Margins point the same way. Nvidia's adjusted gross margin was 74.9%. AMD's was 56%.

What Nvidia has that AMD does not is uncertainty of a different kind. It has an interim chief executive, an investigation its board will not discuss and a quarterly report it has not yet filed. New US export rules bear on its sales to Chinese customers. None of that shows up in earnings. All of it shows up in what investors will pay for them.

The risk in AMD's price is the mirror image. A stock at 31 times next year's earnings needs those earnings to arrive. AMD's forecast for the December quarter is revenue of about $17 billion with an adjusted gross margin of 55%, well below Nvidia's.

What to watch

For Nvidia the next dates are about governance more than sales: a quarterly report due by December 4 and the appointment of a permanent chief executive, which has no date. For AMD it is the December quarter, expected in early February, against $17 billion of revenue and a 55% adjusted gross margin. Wednesday's regular session, which opens at 9:30 a.m. Eastern, is the first full test of the results. If Nvidia's discount is about leadership, a credible appointment should narrow the gap faster than another strong quarter would. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and AMD carry live prices.

Publisher disclosure. TECHi joined Nvidia's Inception program in 2026.

data.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83, adds 155M shares; $81.3B deal uses 99.96% of its limit
data.description:
Anthropic has priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, above the $70 to $78 range it had set, and enlarged the sale by 155 million shares, according to a registration statement the company filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Wednesday evening, November 18, 2026. The offering now stands at 980 million shares worth $81.3 billion. Trading is due to begin on Nasdaq on Thursday, November 19, under the symbol ANT.

The filing also shows how far the company pushed the size. Once an offering is cleared, it can be enlarged through this kind of filing by no more than 20% of the dollar amount first registered. Anthropic used 99.96% of that allowance, TECHi's calculation shows. At $83 the company is worth about $1.10 trillion.

What does the filing say?

The document is short. It registers 178,250,000 more Class A shares, all to be sold by the company, and says that figure includes 23,250,000 shares the underwriters have an option to buy. Its fee table states the initial public offering price as $83.00 a share and puts the value of the added shares at $14.79 billion. It says the SEC declared the main registration statement effective on November 18.

Put that together with the prospectus Anthropic filed on November 17 and the shape of the deal is clear. That prospectus offered 825 million shares, 801,351,354 from the company and 23,648,646 from its seven co-founders, with an option for the banks to buy 123.75 million more. Take the option shares out of the new filing and 155 million are left for the main sale. The base offering becomes 980 million shares. The option grows to 147 million, which is 15% of the base.

At $83, the base offering is worth $81.34 billion. If the banks take their full option it rises to $93.5 billion. Before pricing, the same deal at the middle of its range was worth $61.05 billion. The combination of 19% more shares and a price 12% above the midpoint makes it a third larger. Reuters reported on Wednesday that it is the largest initial public offering on record.

Two documents are still to come. By 7:40 p.m. Eastern on Wednesday Anthropic had not filed its final prospectus, and its newsroom carried no announcement. The share counts here come from the two filings above and TECHi's arithmetic on them.

Why 155 million shares?

Because that is close to the most the rules allowed without starting again. The filing was made under an SEC rule that lets a company add shares to an offering that is already effective, and it takes effect on filing. The limit is 20% of the maximum dollar amount in the original fee table.

Anthropic's original table covered 948.75 million shares at the top of the range, $78, or $74.0 billion. A fifth of that is $14.80 billion. The new filing registers $14.79 billion. The gap is $5.75 million, enough for about 69,000 more shares.

The price worked against the share count. Had the offering priced at $78, the same allowance would have covered 189.75 million extra shares. At $83 it covers 178.3 million. Anthropic registered 178.25 million.

On that evidence the limit on the deal was the rule and not the demand. Anthropic priced above its range and still took nearly every share the allowance permits.

Who gets the money?

Most of it goes to Anthropic. The company is now selling 956,351,354 shares, which brings in $79.4 billion before fees. Seven companies have separately agreed to buy $26.0 billion of non-voting stock at the offering price. Together that is $105.4 billion.

After costs, TECHi estimates Anthropic keeps about $104 billion. The November 17 prospectus put net proceeds at $84.6 billion at a $74 price and said each dollar on the price adds about $793 million. Nine more dollars, plus the 155 million new shares at the same rate, gives $104.5 billion. With the full option it would be about $116.5 billion. The final prospectus will give the company's own figure.

The same sensitivity implies the banks keep about 1% of the price. On the enlarged offering that is roughly $850 million.

The co-founders' sale did not change in shares. Each is selling 3,378,378, as TECHi reported on November 17. At $83 that is $280 million each, up from $250 million at the midpoint, and $1.96 billion between them.

The buyers in the private sale get fewer shares for the same money. Their commitment is fixed in dollars, so $26.0 billion buys 313.3 million shares at $83, against 351.4 million at $74. Google and Nvidia, at about $10.0 billion each, receive about 120.5 million shares apiece. That is 14.7 million fewer than the prospectus illustrated. AMD's $2.5 billion buys 30.1 million. Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft get about 12.0 million each for $1.0 billion, and TSMC about 6.0 million for $500 million.

What is Anthropic worth at $83?

About $1.10 trillion, on TECHi's estimate of 13.20 billion shares outstanding after the offering. That starts from the 13.09 billion in the November 17 prospectus, adds the 155 million new shares and subtracts the 38 million fewer shares issued in the private sale. It is 7% more than the $1.02 trillion the top of the range implied.

Counting stock options, unvested awards and notes that have yet to convert, TECHi's earlier tally of about 17.5 billion shares becomes about 17.6 billion. At $83 that is roughly $1.46 trillion.

The shares sold to the public are 7.4% of the company, up from 6.3%.

The business is growing at a rate that has few precedents and is not yet profitable. Revenue was $33.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, against $2.5 billion a year earlier. The operating loss for the period was $1.26 billion. The net loss was $104.0 billion, of which $94.3 billion was a non-cash charge for the rising value of convertible notes and similar instruments. Revenue in the third quarter alone was $17.0 billion. At $83, investors are paying about 16 times that quarter's revenue multiplied by four. At the midpoint it was 14 times.

The money has a destination. Anthropic's contractual obligations, almost all for computing and infrastructure, total about $900.9 billion. Net proceeds of $104 billion would cover 11.6% of that.

What does it mean for the shares that unlock later?

The release calendar TECHi built from the prospectus still applies, and the bigger offering changes the proportions. Up to 316 million shares held by employees and insiders can be sold from the first day of trading. That is 32% of the enlarged offering, where it was 38% of the original, and it is worth $26.2 billion at $83. By February 2, 2027, up to 1.61 billion shares can become eligible, 1.6 times the offering and $133.8 billion at the offering price.

Those dates assume the final prospectus is dated November 18. If it is, the first timed release after the opening day falls on December 15.

The stock sold in the private placement is outside those agreements, though it is restricted stock that cannot be resold freely at once.

There are two ways to read the pricing. Demand was strong enough to lift the price above the range and fill every additional share, and the company raises about $20 billion more than it planned. Against that, public buyers pay 12% more than the midpoint for the same company, and control stays where it was. A share held by the founders' company carries 50.1% of the votes, and a separate trust elects a majority of the board.

What to watch

The first trade is expected on Thursday, November 19. The final prospectus should follow, with the exact share counts, the net proceeds and the date that fixes the release calendar. The underwriters' option on 147 million shares decides whether the deal ends at $81.3 billion or $93.5 billion. For shareholders of the companies that bought into the private sale, the price sets the cost of their stakes. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and Alphabet carry live prices.

data.title: Oklo to prepay Centrus $35M for reactor fuel; its cash is 72% of its market value
data.description:
Oklo will prepay $35 million to Centrus Energy for enriched uranium and has committed to buy reactor fuel for delivery from 2029 through 2031 on a take-or-pay basis, according to a filing the reactor developer made after the market closed on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The filing attaches the contract itself, five days after the two companies announced the deal without giving figures.

The money is small for Oklo. It is 1.1% of the $3.13 billion in cash and securities the company held at the end of September, TECHi's calculation from its quarterly report shows. The more striking number is what that cash is worth against the stock. It now equals 72% of Oklo's market value, after the shares lost 69% this year.

What does the contract say?

The buyer is Oklo Power SODI, a subsidiary, and the agreement is dated November 11. It covers HALEU, short for high-assay low-enriched uranium. Today's reactors run on uranium enriched to about 5%. Oklo's Aurora reactors, which it calls powerhouses, need fuel enriched to just under 20%, and the contract specifies 19.75%.

Oklo pays the $35 million in two installments. One is due on a fixed date. The other is due when Centrus reaches a commercial milestone, the filing says. Both are credited against later fuel orders. The dates and the size of each installment are redacted in the public copy, as are the quantities and the prices.

What is visible is the shape of the commitment. For the years 2029 to 2031, Oklo must buy a minimum amount of enrichment. The contract calls that obligation "absolute and unconditional". If Oklo takes less, it pays for the shortfall anyway, at the highest unit price in effect that year. If Centrus later sells that fuel to someone else, Oklo gets the net proceeds back, up to what it paid.

Oklo keeps some choices. It can supply its own low-enriched uranium for Centrus to enrich further, if it says so by June 18, 2027. It can supply natural uranium instead if it decides by the last business day of 2027. Otherwise Centrus provides the feed and charges Oklo the market price plus a markup, which is redacted.

The price of the enrichment itself is a base price, also redacted, adjusted for inflation from the first quarter of 2027. The fuel has to be used in US commercial reactors that Oklo or its affiliates own or operate, unless Centrus agrees otherwise. The agreement runs until the end of 2039, or longer if obligations are still open.

What happens if Centrus is late?

This is the part investors could not see until Tuesday. The fuel is meant to come from enrichment capacity that Centrus has not finished building. The contract says so in its opening lines. Oklo agrees to buy what Centrus would supply if it succeeds in building the new facility in Piketon, Ohio.

The contract lists three milestones, all redacted. If any of them slips by more than 12 months, or is abandoned, Oklo can hold back a prepayment that is not yet due, or it can end the contract. If it ends the contract, Centrus refunds 65% of the prepayment it has received. Oklo would lose the other 35%, which is at most $12.25 million if both installments had been paid.

Late deliveries are handled separately. If Centrus misses a delivery by more than 90 days, Oklo can cancel it and buy from another supplier. Centrus then covers Oklo's reasonable extra costs, up to the invoiced price of that delivery plus $10 million. The contract makes that Oklo's only remedy for a missed delivery.

A wider breach that goes uncured for 90 days lets Oklo terminate. That ends the take-or-pay obligation and returns a proportional share of the prepayment. The two sides will also meet every quarter to review progress.

How big is this for Oklo?

Oklo's quarterly report for the three months to September 30 shows $3.13 billion of cash, cash equivalents and marketable debt securities. The $35 million prepayment is 1.1% of that. The company had already prepaid $68.7 million for enriched uranium by the end of September, a line that did not exist at the start of the year. Adding the new $35 million would take fuel prepayments past $100 million.

Oklo has no power plant operating and no power revenue. It had operating expenses of $84.3 million in the quarter and a net loss of $41.7 million, cushioned by $27.9 million of interest income. It aims to deploy its first powerhouse, in Idaho, in 2028 or 2029. That plant is due to run on five metric tons of fuel recovered from a retired government research reactor. The Centrus fuel is for what comes after.

The cash came from shareholders. Oklo sold 32.6 million new shares through at-the-market offerings in the second and third quarters and took in $2.25 billion after costs. That is an average of about $69 a share. The stock closed on Tuesday at $22.38.

At that price, Oklo's 195.3 million shares are worth $4.37 billion. September's cash and securities are 72% of it, or $16.03 a share. On that arithmetic the market is valuing everything else Oklo has, its reactor design, its sites and its customer agreements, at about $1.24 billion.

Why are there two contracts?

Oklo and Centrus signed a letter of intent in June for enough fuel to run up to five Aurora powerhouses for several years. They turned it into more than one contract.

The first, signed on September 30, is tied to Meta. In January, Meta agreed to prepay for power from a 1.2 gigawatt campus that Oklo plans in Pike County, Ohio, to supply Meta's data centers. On November 2, an initial payment from Meta was released from escrow and went straight to Centrus as credit toward fuel orders, Oklo's quarterly report says.

The second, the one filed on Tuesday, has Oklo's subsidiary as the buyer and Oklo making the prepayments. The filing describes it as separate from the Meta-linked agreement. The contract adds that a default under one does not count as a default under the other.

When the companies announced the contracts on November 12, they said deliveries would start in 2029 and gave no dollar amounts. Centrus said it has now secured $5.4 billion of customer contracts and commitments for its new capacity. Its chief executive, Amir Vexler, said Oklo's prepayments would help pay for the expansion. Oklo's chief executive, Jacob DeWitte, said securing fuel was essential to growing beyond the first reactor.

That is the chain investors in AI power are buying. Meta wants electricity for data centers. Oklo needs fuel to make it. Centrus needs its customers' cash to build the plant that makes the fuel. Each link is waiting on the next.

Meta is not alone in looking to nuclear power. In October, Google agreed to anchor an expansion of Constellation Energy's nuclear output, a deal TECHi covered at the time. The difference is that Constellation's reactors exist.

What does it mean for the stocks?

Neither stock has had a good year. Oklo fell 2.8% on Tuesday. It is down 69% in 2026 and 80% below its closing high of $111.65 last December. It fell 5.5% on the day the contracts were announced. Centrus closed at $94.14, down 3.5% on the day and 61% this year. Both rose about 2% in after-hours trading.

The case for Oklo is that it has reserved a scarce input with little cash at risk, and has the money to wait. The case against is that it has signed a take-or-pay contract of undisclosed size for reactors that are not yet built or licensed, with a supplier whose plant is not finished either.

What to watch

Oklo's annual report, due early next year, is the next place to look for the size of the purchase commitment that the redacted contract hides. June 18, 2027 is the first decision date in the contract. Progress at Piketon decides whether the second prepayment is paid at all. TECHi's Oklo quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Nvidia falls 2.9% after record results; it has closed below its open after 9 of 10 reports
data.description:
Nvidia shares fell 2.9% on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, the first full session after the company reported record revenue and raised its growth target for next year. Before the market opened the stock had been up 2.9%. It closed at $150.96, its lowest close since June 2025, according to Nasdaq prices.

The slide fits a pattern, and one detail breaks it. TECHi went through Nvidia's last ten earnings reports. On nine of them the stock finished the next session below the price at which it opened, and on seven it ended lower than it had closed before the results. This time its closest rivals did not fall with it. AMD rose 5.3% and Broadcom 3.6%.

What happened to Nvidia stock on Wednesday?

The results came out after the close on Tuesday. Revenue was $115.84 billion, above the top of Nvidia's own forecast range, and the company guided to $130 billion for the current quarter. The shares rose about 4% in after-hours trading.

They held most of that overnight. Nasdaq's minute-by-minute pre-market data peaks at $161.66 at 5:06 a.m. Eastern, 4.0% above Tuesday's close of $155.46. At 6:39 a.m. the price was $159.89, as TECHi reported this morning.

The gain did not survive the opening bell. Nvidia began regular trading at about $158.94, up 2.2%, and that was close to the best price of the day. The session high was $159.70. By 9:42 a.m. the stock was below Tuesday's close. It fell as low as $150.40 and finished at $150.96. About 339 million shares changed hands.

In market value the move is large. On Nvidia's 24.2 billion diluted shares, the 6:39 a.m. price was worth about $107 billion more than Tuesday's close. The closing price is worth about $109 billion less. The difference between the two, roughly $216 billion, went in under ten hours.

Nvidia has now fallen in seven of the eight sessions since November 6 and is down 19.1% over that stretch. Tuesday's close had already been its lowest in a year. Wednesday's is lower still.

How often does Nvidia fall after earnings?

More often than it rises. Nvidia publishes its results after the market closes, so the next session is the first in which every investor can trade on them. TECHi took the dates of Nvidia's last ten results releases from its SEC filings and compared three Nasdaq prices for each: the close before the results, the next day's open and the next day's close.

On seven of the ten, the stock closed lower the next day than it had before the results. The average move across all ten is a fall of 1.6%.

The pattern inside the day is stronger. On nine of the ten, Nvidia closed below its opening price. Buyers who waited for the open on the morning after paid more than the stock was worth by the close on every occasion but one.

A strong open has not been protection. Nvidia opened at least 2% higher on six of the ten mornings, including Wednesday. On five of those six it closed below its open. The largest reversal was on February 27, 2025, when the stock opened 2.8% higher and closed 8.5% lower. On November 20, 2025 it opened 5.1% higher and closed 3.2% lower.

The exception is the report before this one. On August 27, 2026 the stock opened 6.3% higher and added to the gain, closing up 8.7%.

Across the ten sessions the average move from open to close is a fall of 3.5%. Wednesday's, at 5.0%, is the third-largest of the ten.

Why did AMD and Broadcom rise?

The prices suggest investors are treating Nvidia's problems as Nvidia's own. AMD closed at $530.14, up 5.3%. Broadcom closed at $354.05, up 3.6%. Both sell chips for AI data centers, and Nvidia's results were good news for that market. Its data center revenue rose 110% from a year earlier.

On earlier day-after sessions the stocks tended to move together. AMD fell on four of the six previous days when Nvidia fell, and when it rose it rose less than 1%. Wednesday's gap of 8.2 points in AMD's favour is the widest of the ten.

The rest of the group split. Before the open, the ten AI hardware stocks TECHi tracked this morning were up 4.0% on average. By the close the average gain was 0.7%, and six of the ten finished higher. AMD, Arista Networks and Broadcom gained the most, at 5.3%, 4.0% and 3.6%. CoreWeave, Dell and Marvell lost the most, at 4.1%, 2.9% and 2.2%.

Two of those three depend directly on Nvidia's products. CoreWeave rents out computing capacity that runs on Nvidia chips, and Dell builds them into servers. The stocks that rose most sell alternatives or the networks that connect them.

The four largest spenders on AI data centers did better than they had before the open. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta were up 0.6% on average in pre-market trading. They ended up 1.2% on average, and Amazon did best with a gain of 3.8%. The Nasdaq Composite rose 0.4%.

Since November 6 Nvidia is down 19.1% and AMD is up 18.1%, a gap of 37.2 percentage points. It was 28.8 points at Tuesday's close.

Is the fall about the results?

The numbers Nvidia reported give little reason for it. Revenue beat the top of the forecast range by $5.7 billion. The adjusted gross margin of 74.9% was above the top of its range as well. Interim chief executive Colette Kress raised the company's growth target for next fiscal year to 75% from 70%, as TECHi reported on Tuesday.

There are softer points. The $130 billion outlook covers a 14-week quarter, and per week it implies growth of about 4%, TECHi's analysis of the results showed. Nvidia also forecast a gross margin between 71% and 72%, down from 74.8%.

What the results could not settle is who will run the company. Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive was announced on November 12. The board has said it does not intend to reinstate him and has hired a search firm to find a successor. Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, citing a person familiar with the matter, that the firm has contacted Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm, and has begun approaching other executives. An approach is not an appointment. The board has given no date for one and no update on its investigation.

The valuation gap is wide. At $150.96, Nvidia trades at 9.7 times the earnings analysts expect for the fiscal year that ends in January 2028, on Nasdaq's consensus of $15.55 a share. AMD, at $530.14, trades at 33.1 times its expected 2027 earnings.

The record has limits. Ten reports is a small sample, and each one landed in a different market. Three of the earlier declines came on days when AMD and Broadcom each fell more than 2% as well. Wednesday was not one of those days.

Nor has the pattern reversed quickly. About a month after seven of the nine earlier reports, Nvidia was still below its pre-results close. The two exceptions, in May 2025 and August 2026, followed the two largest day-after gains. That is a record of what happened, and it does not say what will happen this time.

What to watch

The Commerce Department's chip export rule is scheduled to take effect on Thursday, and China has said it will respond. For Nvidia itself the dates are a quarterly report due by December 4 and the naming of a permanent chief executive, which has no date. AMD reports its December quarter in early February. If the discount on Nvidia is about leadership, the next sharp move in the gap is more likely to follow an appointment than a set of numbers. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and AMD carry live prices.

data.title: Everpure revenue jumps 51%, $125M above its forecast; inventory is up fivefold this year
data.description:
Everpure, the data storage company formerly called Pure Storage, reported revenue of $1.46 billion for the three months to November 1, 2026, up 51% from a year earlier, according to results released after the market closed on Wednesday, November 18. That is $125 million above the top of the range the company gave in August. It raised its full-year forecast for the third quarter in a row.

Two details sit behind the headline. Most of the raise is revenue already earned: $130 million of the $155 million added to the full-year midpoint is the amount by which the latest quarter beat its forecast, TECHi's calculation shows. And the growth is absorbing cash. Inventory has grown fivefold since the fiscal year began, to $379 million. The shares rose as much as 6.6% in after-hours trading and were up 2.5% around 5:23 p.m. Eastern.

How did Everpure do against its forecast?

It beat both of the measures it guides. In August the company told investors to expect revenue of $1.325 billion to $1.335 billion and adjusted operating income of $265 million to $275 million. Revenue came in at $1.46 billion. Adjusted operating income was $345 million, $70 million above the top of its range.

Product revenue, which is the sale of storage systems, was $948 million, up 77%. Subscription services revenue was $512 million, up 19%. Annual recurring revenue from subscriptions reached $2.2 billion, up 20%. Remaining performance obligations, the value of contracts not yet counted as revenue, were $4.2 billion, up 44%.

Net income was $100.4 million, or 29 cents a share, against $54.8 million, or 16 cents, a year earlier.

Growth has been speeding up for more than two years. In August Everpure said its revenue growth had accelerated for eight quarters in a row. The latest quarter makes nine. The last five readings are 16%, 20%, 35%, 38% and now 51%.

The company tied part of that to AI. It said it has won a design contract with a second of the five largest hyperscale cloud companies, and that its FlashBlade//EXA system ranked first on every checkpointing and cache measure submitted in MLPerf Storage v3.0, an industry benchmark built around AI workloads. Everpure joined the S&P 500 in September.

What does the new forecast imply?

For the current quarter, which ends around the end of January, Everpure expects revenue of $1.50 billion to $1.52 billion and adjusted operating income of $350 million to $360 million. For the full fiscal year it now expects revenue of $5.20 billion to $5.21 billion, up from $5.03 billion to $5.07 billion, and adjusted operating income of $1.08 billion to $1.09 billion, up from $940 million to $960 million.

The midpoint of the revenue forecast rose by $155 million. The quarter just reported beat the midpoint of its own forecast by $130 million. So 84% of the raise is money that has already come in.

The rest is the change to the quarter ahead. The old full-year forecast left about $1.48 billion for the fourth quarter, on TECHi's arithmetic. The new midpoint is $1.51 billion, about 2% higher.

That forecast also implies a slowdown. Revenue of $1.51 billion would be 3.4% more than the quarter just reported, which was itself 23% more than the one before. Measured against a year earlier it is growth of 42% to 43%, down from 51%. If that is what happens, it ends the run of acceleration.

Everpure's recent record suggests the range is cautious. To keep growth above 51%, it would need fourth-quarter revenue of about $1.60 billion, which is $83 million above the top of the new range. It beat the top of its range by $125 million this quarter and by $81 million in the quarter before.

Chief financial officer Tarek Robbiati said in the release that the company is also standing by a preliminary outlook for the fiscal year after this one. The release does not give those figures.

Where is the cash going?

Into components. Everpure builds its systems around flash memory. The company said in its quarterly report in September that components had become scarce and more costly, and that it raised its own prices in the first half of the fiscal year in response.

The cost shows in the margin. Gross margin was 68.0%, down from 72.3% a year earlier. On product sales alone it was 66.7%, against 71.6%, TECHi's calculation from the income statement shows. The cost of product revenue more than doubled while product revenue rose 77%.

The trend within the year is better. Product gross margin was 64.5% in the first quarter and 65.3% in the second before reaching 66.7%, which suggests the price increases are catching up with costs.

The larger effect is on the balance sheet. Inventory was $379.5 million on November 1. Three months earlier it was $106.3 million, and at the start of the fiscal year it was $75.9 million. Building it took $272 million of cash in the quarter.

A second line has grown as well. Prepaid expenses and other current assets stood at $967 million, against $356 million when the year began. The release does not break that down. In the September report most of the equivalent balance, $904 million of $1.03 billion, was money owed mainly by Everpure's contract manufacturers for components that Everpure bought itself and sold on to them, together with tax-related receivables. In other words the company has been buying parts itself and passing them to the manufacturers that assemble its systems.

Inventory and that line together come to $1.35 billion, $915 million more than at the start of the year. Part of that is unpaid bills, as accounts payable rose by $325 million. Cash and marketable securities fell to $1.14 billion from $1.55 billion.

Free cash flow recovered in the quarter, to $265 million from an outflow of $238 million in the one before. Over nine months it is $139 million, against $414 million in the same period last year, while revenue rose 42%. Capital spending in the quarter was $178 million, close to three times the level of a year earlier.

Everpure is not alone in committing cash to secure parts. Nvidia's supply commitments have reached $390 billion, most of it for memory, as TECHi reported earlier on Wednesday.

How did the stock react?

Unevenly. Everpure closed at $101.00 on Wednesday, down 0.8%, before the results. In after-hours trading it rose as high as $107.70 at 4:12 p.m. Eastern, a gain of 6.6%, according to Nasdaq's minute-by-minute data. Around 5:23 p.m. it was near $103.53, up 2.5%. After-hours trading is thin, and the company's call with analysts began at 5 p.m. Eastern. This report does not include it.

The stock's history after results is a warning against reading much into the first move. Everpure fell the day after each of its last four reports, by 27.3% last December, 10.3% in February, 14.8% in May and 8.9% in August, Nasdaq prices show. Each of those releases also said results had exceeded the top of the company's guidance.

The shares are still up 51% this year. They are 36% below their closing high of $156.97, set on October 13. At Wednesday's close the company was worth about $35 billion on its diluted share count. That is 6.8 times the revenue it forecasts for this fiscal year and about 33 times its forecast adjusted operating income.

There is a case on each side. Growth has accelerated for nine quarters, recurring revenue is $2.2 billion, and two of the largest cloud companies have chosen its technology. Against that, margins are lower than a year ago, cash is tied up in parts, and the forecast points to slower growth.

What to watch

Everpure's quarterly report, due in the coming weeks, will show what is inside its inventory and receivables. The fourth quarter will show whether revenue lands near the $1.51 billion it forecast or the $1.60 billion that would keep growth accelerating. Component prices will decide how much of that revenue it keeps as margin. TECHi's Everpure quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Nvidia rules out Huang’s return and lifts growth target to 75%; that needs 18% a quarter
data.description:
Nvidia's board does not intend to bring Jensen Huang back as chief executive, chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of the company's earnings call on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, according to CNBC and CBS News. On the same call, held after Nvidia reported its results, interim chief executive Colette Kress raised the company's revenue growth forecast for its next fiscal year to 75% from 70%.

The forecast is larger than it sounds. On TECHi's calculation it puts revenue for the year to January 2028 at about $741 billion, which is $318 billion more than this year. To get there from the quarter Nvidia has just guided, sales would have to grow about 18% every quarter. The outlook for the current quarter implies 4%. Nvidia shares were up about 4% in after-hours trading.

What did the board say about Jensen Huang?

Jones, the board's new chairman, opened the call himself. Huang's resignation was announced on November 12. CNBC quoted Jones as saying the board had accepted it unanimously and "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO". CBS News reported the same statement.

He also gave the first detail on what comes next. The board has hired the search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent chief executive, CNBC reported. It is considering candidates from inside and outside the company and has every confidence in Kress in the meantime, according to CBS News.

Jones did not take questions on the circumstances of the resignation or on the board's investigation, and said the board would say more when appropriate, Scripps News reported. None of the accounts of the call reports a date for an appointment.

The statement came hours after Huang said publicly that he would return if the board decided it was in the company's interest, CBS News reported. The board's answer was no.

Kress, for her part, told analysts that the business is running as usual and that customers, suppliers and partners are behind the company, according to Scripps News. Analysts cited by CNBC said the financial effect of the change at the top is unlikely to show before the end of fiscal 2028, because most of next year's revenue is already under contract.

That settles one of the two things Nvidia's results release and written commentary left open. TECHi's report on the results noted that they gave no update on the investigation and no timetable for a successor. The call added a search firm. The accounts of it do not include a timetable.

What did Kress forecast?

The quarter she reported was strong. Revenue was $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier and $7.8 billion above the midpoint of Nvidia's own forecast. Nvidia formally guides one quarter at a time, and for the current quarter it expects revenue of $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%.

On the call Kress went further. Investors had wondered whether Nvidia would drop an earlier forecast of 70% growth for the fiscal year that ends in January 2028, CNBC reported. She raised it to 75%. She tied her confidence to supply, saying the chips, the advanced packaging and the memory Nvidia needs are all coming together.

Other details come from news accounts of the call. A transcript was not yet available on Tuesday evening. Kress pointed to a backlog of $2.5 trillion across the cloud industry, up from $2 trillion three months ago, and said contracts for Nvidia's older Hopper chips are being renewed at up to twice their original prices, according to investingLive. She said Nvidia intends to return all of its excess free cash flow to shareholders. The product schedule is unchanged, with the next version of its Rubin systems due next year and a new design called Feynman in 2028, the same account says.

On the chip export rule the Commerce Department issued on Monday, Kress said Nvidia would study it and that demand still far exceeds supply, CBS News reported. Nvidia put the small fall in its gross margin last quarter down to the start of production of its Rubin chips, as its written commentary had said. TECHi has not seen a reason given for the larger fall it forecasts.

What does 75% growth require?

Start with this year. Nvidia has reported $293.7 billion of revenue for the first nine months of fiscal 2027. Add the $130.0 billion it expects this quarter and the year comes to $423.7 billion. That is 96% more than the $215.9 billion of fiscal 2026.

Growth of 75% on top of that is $741 billion. The step up from 70% to 75% is worth about $21 billion by itself. In dollars it would be the biggest increase Nvidia has ever attempted: $318 billion in one year, against $208 billion this year. Nvidia grew 65% in fiscal 2026. A 75% year would be slower than this one in percentage terms and far bigger in money. It works out to an average of $185 billion a quarter, 60% more than the record quarter Nvidia reported on Tuesday.

The calendar makes the task slightly harder. Fiscal 2027 has 53 weeks and fiscal 2028 has 52. Per week, the forecast is growth of 78%.

The harder part is the starting point. The current quarter's outlook works out to $9.29 billion a week, or $120.7 billion for a normal 13-week quarter. As TECHi showed earlier on Tuesday, that is only 4.2% above last quarter's weekly rate. If Nvidia kept growing at 4.2% a quarter, fiscal 2028 would come to about $536 billion, an increase of 26%.

To reach $741 billion, revenue has to grow 17.9% in each of the next four quarters. That would take quarterly revenue from the equivalent of $120.7 billion now to $233 billion in the final quarter of fiscal 2028. Nvidia has done it before. It grew 18% in the second quarter of this year and 20% in the third. The forecast says, in effect, that the slower quarter it has just guided is the exception.

A better current quarter would help only a little. Nvidia beat its last forecast by 7.3%. If it did the same again, this year's total would rise too, and the growth needed each quarter would still be 15.8%.

What does it mean for Nvidia stock?

Nvidia closed on Tuesday at $155.46, before the results. In the six sessions to Monday, the shares had lost about $735 billion of market value, as TECHi reported on Tuesday morning. At that price the company is worth about $3.76 trillion on its diluted share count, or five times the revenue the new forecast implies for fiscal 2028.

The case for the stock is that the forecast was raised in the same week the founder left, and that Kress backed it with supply contracts and a promise of more cash for shareholders. By Kress's account, customers are paying more for old chips, not less.

The case against is everything the call did not resolve. Nvidia has an interim chief executive, a search that has only just started and an investigation its chairman will not discuss. Its quarterly report has not been filed. A new export rule is days old. And a full-year forecast given on a call is not the same as guidance, which Nvidia still gives for one quarter only.

What to watch

The quarterly report is due by December 4 and is where Nvidia must describe legal proceedings. Huang has agreed to appear before House lawmakers on December 1, CBS News reported. The next results, expected in late February, bring the first test. A first-quarter outlook near $142 billion would be on the path to 75%. TECHi's Nvidia quote page carries the live price.
